speaker: Tim Latimer
title: Tim Latimer on Solving the Financing Problem for Geothermal
question: In enhanced geothermal development, what makes adapting horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing from oil and gas fundamentally harder than applying them in shale?
guest: I actually started my career as a drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry, and there's a lot of technology overlap between oil and gas and geothermal. The technological gap of getting high flow rates out of low-permeability formations really was the exact same whenever you looked at geothermal. That's what held shale back, and that's what was holding geothermal back. But taking that technique and applying it to geothermal has involved an enormous amount of technical work because there's a lot different. The first thing is we look for much higher temperatures. The Eagle Ford in South Texas is considered very hot for an onshore oil and gas basin, but it's only like 300 degrees Fahrenheit, which is considered cold for geothermal. We're now drilling up to 440 degrees Fahrenheit, and that has taken enormous tech development. It also turns out that geologically hot places very often overlap with granite, which is a much harder rock type than shale. So we had to develop techniques to deal with a much more challenging engineering environment where the rock is harder, the temperatures are hotter, and the operation of the reservoir is very different.

The core difficulty is that the rock and the goal are both different. Shale is soft, sedimentary, and relatively cool; geothermal targets are hard, abrasive crystalline rock such as granite at roughly 200°C or more. That slows drilling, wears out bits quickly, and pushes downhole electronics, motors, steering tools, packers, cements and casing past the temperature limits they were designed for, while thermal cycling stresses the well's integrity.

The fracturing objective is also harder. In shale, you only need fractures that let hydrocarbons drain to a single well once. In enhanced geothermal, you must create a durable fracture network that connects an injection well to a production well and circulates water through it continuously for decades. Flow must be spread evenly across many fractures: if one dominant path takes most of the flow, the water "short-circuits," cooling that path quickly and ruining heat output. Operators also need to limit water loss into the formation, keep fractures open at high temperature, and manage induced seismicity, since stimulation in stressed basement rock often works by shearing natural fractures.

Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) face far harsher geological, thermal, and hydraulic demands than shale operations. Whereas shale is relatively soft, layered sedimentary rock, EGS targets deep, hard, abrasive crystalline rock like granite, which destroys drill bits, slows drilling rates, and lacks clear bedding planes for steering. Simultaneously, temperatures exceeding 200°C to 300°C degrade conventional directional-steering electronics, downhole motors, elastomer seals, zonal-isolation packers, and proppants, which can crush or chemically dissolve under extreme heat and closure stress.

Equally important, the reservoir goal is fundamentally different. A shale well simply drains hydrocarbons into a single borehole, so irregular fractures still produce effectively. EGS must instead engineer a connected heat exchanger between separate injection and production wells. Stimulated fractures must intersect both wells while distributing flow evenly across vast rock surfaces for decades; if water channels into a few dominant pathways—a feedback worsened as cooling rock contracts and widens those fractures—cold fluid bypasses hot rock, causing premature thermal short-circuiting. Finally, pressuring stiff, critically stressed basement rock near pre-existing faults carries higher risks of fluid loss and felt induced seismicity.

noweb.answer:
Adapting shale techniques to enhanced geothermal systems is fundamentally harder due to extreme rock mechanics, intense heat, and unforgiving flow-loop requirements. Whereas shale is relatively soft, layered sedimentary rock, geothermal targets are typically deep, hard, abrasive crystalline rocks like granite, which drastically slow drilling and rapidly destroy bits. Meanwhile, reservoir temperatures often exceed 200°C to 300°C—far hotter than typical shale plays—degrading directional steering electronics, elastomeric seals, fracturing fluids, and standard quartz proppants, which can crush or chemically dissolve in hot brines. 

Most importantly, the reservoir objective is entirely different. A shale well only needs fractures connected to a single wellbore for one-way hydrocarbon drainage, whereas enhanced geothermal must circulate fluid continuously between separate injection and production wells to sweep heat evenly. Stimulating stressed crystalline rock tends to reactivate existing faults rather than creating uniform planar fractures, heightening induced seismicity risks and causing hydraulic short-circuits where water rushes through one dominant channel, cooling it prematurely and stranding the surrounding thermal energy.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Shale techniques were built for soft, layered sedimentary rock at modest temperatures. EGS targets hot crystalline basement rock, usually granite, at 175–250°C or more, and that changes nearly every part of the job.

The rock is hard and abrasive. It wears out bits and slows drilling, so wells take longer and cost more. The heat damages the downhole electronics used for steering and measurement while drilling, along with elastomer seals, drilling mud and cement. Thermal cycling also stresses the casing.

The bigger problem is that the fractures have a different job. In shale, a fracture only has to release oil or gas into one well, once, and it doesn't matter much if production falls off quickly. In EGS, fractures must link an injection well to a production well so water can circulate through hot rock for decades. The flow has to spread evenly across many fractures. If it short-circuits through a few, those paths cool quickly and the well's heat output falls. Fractures in crystalline rock are also hard to predict, because they follow the existing natural fractures and stress conditions.

Finally, heat is worth less per well than oil. EGS wells need very high flow rates to pay off, and the industry has to manage the risk of triggering earthquakes, as happened at Basel and Pohang.

Adapting oil and gas techniques to enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) is fundamentally harder because EGS faces far harsher rock and heat conditions alongside a more demanding flow goal. Whereas shale is relatively soft sedimentary rock at moderate temperatures, EGS targets deep, hard, abrasive crystalline rock like granite at temperatures often exceeding 200 °C. That extreme heat degrades downhole directional electronics, elastomers, motors, and fracturing fluids, while the hard basement rock rapidly wears drill bits, slows penetration, and complicates steering horizontal wells.

Hydraulic fracturing also serves a different purpose. In shale, operators stimulate a single well to drain trapped hydrocarbons. In EGS, stimulation must build an evenly distributed fracture network linking separate injection and production wells to circulate water continuously for decades. In stressed crystalline rock, injected fluid often slips along existing natural fractures rather than opening uniform new ones, raising the risk of induced seismicity and thermal short-circuiting, where water rushes through a few dominant paths and cools the reservoir too quickly.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
In shale, hydraulic fracturing creates paths for oil and gas to flow from the rock into a production well. In enhanced geothermal, those fractures have to form a heat exchanger between an injection well and a production well. Water must circulate at high rates across enough hot rock to sustain useful temperatures for years. A poorly connected fracture network restricts flow, while a highly conductive shortcut can send water back to the production well before it picks up enough heat.

Geothermal targets are often hotter, harder crystalline rock, which accelerates bit wear and pushes downhole tools toward their temperature limits. Existing fractures and local stresses can also make stimulation harder to predict. The challenge is to control where the water flows and how much rock it contacts while managing water loss and induced seismicity.

In shale, the hydrocarbons are already in the rock. A horizontal well and hydraulic fractures give them a short path into the well. In enhanced geothermal systems, the heat is in the rock, but extracting it requires water to circulate between an injection well and a production well. The fractures must connect the wells and expose enough hot rock to sustain heat transfer. Too little connectivity limits flow. A single highly conductive shortcut can deliver plenty of water but cool quickly, leaving much of the reservoir’s heat untapped.

Creating that underground heat exchanger also means drilling long laterals through hot, often hard and abrasive crystalline rock. The rock wears down drill bits, high temperatures strain downhole tools, and stimulation can reactivate faults. Success depends on sustaining both flow and temperature for years.
